title: New device captures carbon dioxide by pumping it across a battery
gist: A University of Delaware team, linked to startup RepAir Carbon, demonstrated a battery-like nickel hydroxide electrochemical cell that captures CO2 using about 0.8 MWh per ton versus 1.5-3 MWh for current direct air capture, and projects costs falling from $566 to $92 per ton at 1,000x pilot scale.

insights.claim: A team led by James Buchen of the University of Delaware demonstrated a battery-based electrochemical carbon-capture technique that may require less energy and be cheaper than dominant reversible-filter designs.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: A lower-energy capture route could reshape the cost curve of direct air capture.
insights.locator: It’s also possible to do a similar

insights.claim: The device uses nickel hydroxide for both electrodes: hydroxide made at the cathode converts CO2 to carbonate, which crosses a membrane to the lower-pH anode and reverts to CO2; reversing voltage swaps the electrode roles.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Using cheap, established battery chemistry may ease manufacturing scale-up.

insights.claim: A nine-cell lab-scale stack used about 0.8 MWh of electricity per ton of captured CO2, compared with roughly 1.5 to 3 MWh per ton at current direct air capture facilities.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Roughly halving energy use would cut the largest operating cost of carbon removal.
insights.quote: This small device used electricity at a rate of about 0.8 megawatt-hours per ton of captured CO2.

insights.claim: Researchers affiliated with startup RepAir Carbon estimate an initial pilot plant cost of about $566 per ton, falling to $92 per ton at 1,000 times pilot capacity using lithium-ion battery learning rates.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: If achieved, sub-$100 capture would be a step change for carbon-removal markets.
insights.quote: they estimate they could get to $92 per ton of captured CO2

insights.claim: Climeworks aims for $250-350 per ton by 2030 and has shown how hard it is to meet optimistic scaling projections.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Investors should discount startup cost projections given industry track record.
insights.quote: has demonstrated how difficult it can be to meet optimistic scaling projections

insights.claim: Reaching $100 per ton has long been the carbon-capture industry's goal because costs that low could spur much wider adoption, and more competing technologies improve the odds someone gets there.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: $100/ton is the key threshold for commercial carbon-removal demand.
insights.quote: Targeting $100 per ton has long been the goal in the carbon-capture world
